Sparse attention mechanisms — whether learned (BigBird, Longformer) or dynamic (Routing Transformers, Mixture-of-Experts attention) — commit to structural priors about which positions attend to which: local windows, global tokens, strided patterns, or router-selected clusters. The central question is what happens when the distribution of input lengths at inference time diverges from the distribution seen during training, specifically whether the specialized roles that individual heads develop (syntactic boundary detection, coreference linking, long-range retrieval) remain functionally coherent or collapse into redundant, overlapping, or entirely inert behavior. Experts worry about a failure mode beginners consistently miss: head specialization is not an intrinsic property of a head's parameters — it is an emergent property of the interaction between those parameters and the attention pattern the head is permitted to execute, so when pattern geometry changes (e.g., a local window that covered 12% of tokens at length 512 now covers 1.2% at length 5120), the head's effective receptive field collapses and the functional role dissolves without any weight change. The retrieval failure this produces is insidious because perplexity and even aggregate benchmark scores can remain stable — the model compensates via other heads or layers — while specific structured retrieval tasks (e.g., resolving a coreference introduced 3,000 tokens back) silently degrade. Concretely, Olsson et al.'s induction head work and follow-on mechanistic interpretability research show that even a two-head induction circuit depends on positional geometry being preserved; stretch that geometry and the circuit breaks, but nothing in the loss surface signals the breakage until you probe for it directly.

The critical geometric property is the effective rank and isotropy of the query-key inner product distribution across the position-offset axis — specifically, whether the head's Q and K projection matrices have learned a low-rank subspace that is selective (high variance along a few offset-correlated directions) versus diffuse (variance spread across many directions uncorrelated with positional offset). A retrieval head that degrades gracefully has concentrated its query-key alignment signal into directions that remain discriminative even when the set of candidate key positions expands; a head that collapses catastrophically has learned to rely on the absolute scarcity of attendable positions (the sparse mask doing the selection work) rather than the intrinsic Q-K geometry doing it. Mathematically, you can measure this without running the full model by computing the singular value spectrum of W_Q^T W_K and examining how much of the total spectral energy is captured by the top-k singular vectors — heads where the top-1 singular value captures >60% of energy (highly anisotropic) tend to be positionally discriminative by geometry, while flat spectra indicate mask-dependent selection. Elhage et al. (2021) and follow-on work from Anthropic's transformer circuits thread show that induction heads exhibit precisely this anisotropy: their Q-K subspace has a near-rank-1 structure aligned with the previous-token offset direction. Praktically, Noci et al. (2022) in "Signal Propagation in Transformers" and Dong et al.'s rank collapse analysis provide the theoretical grounding: when attention logit variance is low (flat Q-K spectrum), softmax concentrates or flattens pathologically under sequence length shift, destroying the retrieval signal entirely. You can therefore pre-screen heads for length-generalization fragility by computing the participation ratio of the W_Q^T W_K singular value distribution on weight matrices alone — heads with participation ratio near 1 are robust; heads near the full rank are mask-dependent and will collapse when the mask geometry changes.

Fine-tuning on longer sequences can rescue mask-dependent retrieval heads, but only under a narrow condition: the head must receive direct, non-redundant gradient signal before other heads preempt the functional role, and in practice this window closes faster than most practitioners expect. The gradient into W_Q and W_K for a retrieval head is proportional to the outer product of the attention-weighted value error and the attending query/key activations — when the head's attention is diffuse (flat Q-K spectrum producing near-uniform softmax), this gradient is small and poorly directed, because the error signal is spread across all positions rather than concentrated at the retrieval target, producing a near-zero update to the very subspace that needs restructuring. Meanwhile, other heads with sharper Q-K geometry receive larger, better-conditioned gradients and adapt first, effectively absorbing the retrieval function; once this redistribution stabilizes (often within the first few hundred steps of continued pretraining, per observations in Geva et al. 2022 on feed-forward key reuse and Jain et al.'s work on attention head redundancy), the originally specialized head's gradient signal collapses further because the loss no longer depends on it — a form of gradient shadowing. The contrast case — a head with anisotropic Q-K spectrum encountering length shift — shows a qualitatively different gradient: the error concentrates at missed retrieval targets, the gradient aligns with the existing dominant singular direction of W_Q^T W_K, and fine-tuning sharpens rather than restructures the subspace, which is why continued pretraining rescues performance for models like LLaMA being extended from 2K to 32K context (Fu et al. 2023, "Data Engineering for Scaling Language Models"). Critically, you can distinguish the two regimes before fine-tuning by examining whether the gradient on the first long-context batch projects significantly onto the top singular vectors of W_Q^T W_K — if the projection is weak (<10% of gradient norm in that subspace), functional cession is likely already underway and the head will not recover without explicit regularization or head-specific learning rate scaling to overcome the gradient shadowing.

Concretely, you compute the average pairwise cosine similarity of a head's output vectors across a batch of diverse long-context inputs — ceded heads typically show cosine similarity >0.95 across inputs where a functional retrieval head would show <0.4, a gap large enough to detect with a few hundred forward passes without any labels or probing classifiers. A complementary signal is query vector entropy in the projected subspace: for a ceded head, query vectors from semantically distant inputs occupy nearly the same region of the Q-projection space (low inter-input dispersion), whereas a live retrieval head produces query vectors that spread across its dominant singular directions in direct response to what the input is asking to retrieve. Ferrando et al. The practical recipe is therefore a two-signal screen: output cosine similarity across inputs above 0.9 AND attention entropy above 0.8 * log(sequence_length) simultaneously flags ceded heads with low false-positive rate, detectable in a single inference pass over a diagnostic batch before any retrieval benchmark is run.

Surgical inference-time reactivation is possible in principle and has been partially demonstrated, but the failure modes are severe enough that it should be understood as a diagnostic tool rather than a production fix. The most direct intervention is attention pattern replacement: instead of letting the ceded head compute its own diffuse attention, you substitute a pattern derived from an external retrieval signal (BM25 scores, dense retrieval similarities, or a smaller probe model) and let the head's V projection and output matrix operate normally — this was explored implicitly in Retrieval-Augmented Attention work and explicitly in Ye et al. (2023) "Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding," where injecting structured attention patterns into specific heads recovered factual retrieval performance without weight changes. The first and most common failure mode is value subspace mismatch: the V projection of a ceded head has co-adapted to produce outputs compatible with the residual stream given diffuse attention, so forcing a sharp retrieval pattern causes it to read out a value combination that was never seen during training, producing an output vector that lies off the manifold of normal residual stream updates and destabilizes downstream layers — empirically this manifests as attention entropy spikes or logit distribution flattening in the next 2-3 layers. The second failure mode is functional redundancy inversion: if another head has already absorbed the retrieval role during gradient shadowing, reactivating the ceded head creates two competing retrieval signals in the residual stream, and because transformer layers sum these additively, the interference can degrade retrieval performance below the ceded baseline, particularly when the two heads retrieve slightly different candidates for the same query. A subtler third failure mode involves positional encoding entanglement: ceded heads in RoPE-based models (LLaMA, Mistral) have their V projections shaped by the rotational position encoding applied during their training-distribution forward passes; injecting an out-of-distribution attention pattern breaks the implicit positional contract the V matrix expects, producing systematic retrieval position errors that are hard to diagnose because outputs look plausible but point to wrong sequence offsets. The cleanest partial success in the literature is activation patching from mechanistic interpretability (Wang et al. 2022 on the IOI circuit, Meng et al. ROME): patching specific layer outputs rather than raw attention patterns sidesteps value mismatch by operating in the residual stream directly, but this requires knowing exactly which activation carries the retrieval signal, which defeats the purpose of a general reactivation procedure.
